questions.q: In the worked ticket-classifier example, what was the recommended fix for tickets mentioning both billing and a bug?
options: Rewrite the entire prompt from scratch
Add one sentence resolving the specific ambiguity, then re-run the full test set
Lower the classifier's required accuracy threshold
Remove billing as a valid category entirely
questions.explain: The lesson's recommended move was a targeted, single addition addressing the specific ambiguity, followed by a full re-run to check for regressions.

questions.q: Which four ingredients does this lesson say a strong prompt carries?
options: Model name, temperature, token limit, and system role
Task, Context, Format, and Constraints
Grammar, spelling, punctuation, and length
Greeting, question, politeness, and sign-off
questions.explain: The four ingredients covered are Task, Context, Format, and Constraints — what to do, for whom, in what shape, and within what limits.

questions.q: Why does "Be extremely detailed, but keep your answer under 50 words" tend to produce inconsistent results?
options: It's a missing-output-format failure
The two requirements conflict, and the model has to silently pick a winner each time
The word "detailed" is not a word models recognize
50 words is too long for any model to generate
questions.explain: "Extremely detailed" and "under 50 words" can't both be fully satisfied for most topics, so the model resolves the conflict inconsistently run to run.

questions.q: Why is "You are a helpful assistant" considered a weak system prompt?
options: It is too long for most models to process
It's already close to the model's default behavior and gives it no real new information
It is grammatically incorrect
It uses a forbidden word that triggers a content filter
questions.explain: The phrase doesn't specify a role, scope, boundary, or rule — it's not wrong, just empty of anything the model couldn't already assume.

questions.q: What does chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting ask the model to do?
options: Reason step by step before giving a final answer
Generate several unrelated answers at once
Translate the question into another language first
Skip straight to the shortest possible answer
questions.explain: Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to work through its reasoning before stating a final answer, rather than jumping straight to a conclusion.

options: Breaking one large task into a sequence of smaller prompts, where each step's output feeds the next step's input
Sending the exact same prompt to the model multiple times in a row
Combining as many instructions as possible into a single prompt
A technique for reducing the number of tokens in a single prompt
questions.explain: Prompt chaining splits an overloaded task into focused steps, with each step's output becoming the next step's input.

questions.q: What does role-based prompting change, according to this lesson?
options: Only the formatting of the output, nothing else
Vocabulary, priorities, and depth — not just tone
Only the length of the response
Nothing measurable — it is purely cosmetic
questions.explain: Assigning a role shifts what the model treats as important and how deeply it explores a given point, not just the surface tone of the reply.

questions.q: In the lesson's train-distance example, why did the majority vote land on 195 miles instead of 185?
options: 195 was simply the first answer generated
The question was rewritten between runs
Two of the three independent runs agreed on 195; one run made an arithmetic slip and got 185
185 is not a valid number for a distance
questions.explain: Two out of three sampled runs converged on 195 miles; the outvoted run's arithmetic mistake was overridden by the majority.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 'fixed cost' from a 'variable cost' in a context budget?
options: Fixed costs are always larger than variable costs
Variable costs don't count against the token limit
There is no real difference between the two
Fixed costs (system prompt, tool schemas) don't change call to call; variable costs (history, retrieval) grow and need an explicit cap
questions.explain: Fixed costs are constant and measured once; variable costs grow over time and must be capped or they eventually consume the whole budget.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say precision and brevity usually aren't in tension when writing a tool description?
options: Because a precise description is usually also a short one, while a vague one often runs long without saying anything specific
Because precise descriptions are always written in a different language
Because brevity is more important than precision in all cases
Because tool descriptions are never read by the model, only by developers
questions.explain: The lesson notes that being specific (trigger condition, parameter format) tends to produce concise text, while vague descriptions often ramble without adding useful detail.

questions.q: A response comes back wrong. What does this lesson say you should ask first?
options: Whether to switch to a different model entirely
Whether the user typed their question correctly
Nothing — always reword the prompt first regardless of cause
Whether the instruction itself was unclear, or whether it was clear but buried under irrelevant context
questions.explain: The lesson's core practical point: distinguishing a prompt problem from a context problem determines which fix actually addresses the cause.

questions.q: What is the key risk of truncation compared to rolling summarization?
options: Anything only mentioned in a dropped turn is genuinely gone, not just compressed into a summary
Truncation always costs more tokens than summarization
Truncation requires an extra model call to run
Truncation cannot be used on conversation history, only on documents
questions.explain: Truncation drops turns outright with no summary, so information unique to those turns is lost entirely, unlike summarization which retains a compact version of it.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how should a full eval suite be re-run when shipping a prompt change?
options: Only the specific case the change targeted needs to be re-checked
Re-running the suite is optional if the developer is confident in the change
Only cases added in the last week need to be re-run
The entire suite should be re-run on every ship, not just cases related to what changed
questions.explain: The lesson states the full suite should be re-run on every ship, since a change can affect behavior on cases that seem unrelated to what was targeted.

questions.q: In the reported result ({prompt_a_pass_rate: 0.738, prompt_b_pass_rate: 0.929, winner: "B", reason: "fewer policy violations"}), why does the specific 'reason' field matter?
options: It doesn't matter — only the pass rates are useful
It is required by JSON syntax and has no functional purpose
It replaces the need to run the eval set at all
It gives a specific, checkable explanation for the win, rather than a vague impression that B 'reads better'
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes that a trustworthy A/B result reports a specific, checkable reason for the outcome, not just a subjective sense that one version seemed better.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say LLM-as-judge grading still needs a human spot-check in the loop?
options: Because LLM judges are never allowed to grade anything
Because human review is always faster than automated grading
Because a judge model can drift or develop blind spots over time, the same way any single evaluator can
Because LLM-as-judge only works on exact-match cases
questions.explain: The lesson explains that periodic human review of a sample of judged cases catches systematic errors an LLM judge may develop over time, which pure automation wouldn't catch on its own.

questions.q: In the real eval case shown ({id, category, input, expected_behavior}), what does the expected_behavior field represent?
options: The literal text the user typed
A unique identifier for the case
The name of the model being tested
The defined standard the actual output is graded against
questions.explain: expected_behavior (or an exact expected output, for cases with one correct answer) is the standard used to judge whether the model's actual response passed.

questions.q: What is the stated goal of this capstone?
options: To memorize every lesson title from Chapters 1-4
To pick the shortest possible use case to minimize effort
To prove you can build a tested, versioned, genuinely evaluated prompt library around a real use case of your own choosing
To rewrite the course outline file
questions.explain: The kickoff frames the capstone as applying the course's full pipeline — prompts, context, and evaluation — to a real use case, producing real results rather than a guided walkthrough.

questions.q: What does the lesson say is more convincing than a slide deck when presenting this capstone?
options: A real, working prompt library, walked through live — including a live automated test run
A verbal description of what the prompt library would contain
A single screenshot of the folder structure
Reciting the course outline from memory
questions.explain: The lesson's core advice is that a real, running project — including running the automated test live and reporting the actual pass rate — is far more convincing than describing one.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what should results/ (inside evals/) actually contain?
options: The actual output of running the automated testing loop, one file per test run
A written description of what testing would probably show
A copy of the eval_set.json file with no changes
Marketing copy about the prompt library
questions.explain: The lesson specifies results/ holds the real output of Lesson 19's automated testing loop for each run — actual results, not a description of expected results.
